title: My AI-assisted game hit 50 reviews (85% positive) and 1,500 copies sold. Here's what I learned about Steam, refunds and community
author: Shalke97
selftext:
Hello guys,

after 50 reviews and 1500 sold copies I want to celebrate a bit, but also give something back. Developing the game, releasing it and updating it constantly taught me a lot about Steam and about how important a community really is. I know we have the new rules here about sharing your workflow, but mainly this sub should be about sharing experiences as a whole. Most of us have AI Development figured out, but most of you haven't released a game to Steam yet. Thats why i want to share this with you, as this is as important as making a good game! 

First of all, I really want to put emphasis on how important it is to be good at receiving feedback and critique. My launch was rocky and with that came some negative reviews. Instead of panicking I decided to stay calm and handle every piece of feedback professionally, even though internally I was deeply worried everything might fail. Which is a reasonable reaction lol.

My refund rate at the beginning was pretty high, around 27%. Now it sits at 15%. Nearly halved. So what did I do to get there? The answer is shockingly simple.

Don't have a community.. instead, be part of the community.

A lot of my positive reviews mention how interactive I am with the players. I answer every thread in the discussions. When someone reports a bug I fix it and then go back and tell them it's fixed. A few people actually changed their negative review to a positive one after that, which honestly felt better than the sales numbers. Most of the early refunds came from an early issue that i overlooked. And funnily enough i was not fast enough to fix it in time. When i woke up next morning, there were 3 negative reviews naming the same problem, and I couldn't undo that, but I could show people the game is alive and that someone is listening. So thats what i did, while i set up my Agent to fight those issues, i made sure to prioritize to make an public announcement to let players know, i'm working on everything they reported.



If I could do it again I would do a playtest before releasing, to have a smoother launch. Would have saved me a lot of those early refunds. My next Game won't have those issues, because i know better now and you should too! 



Game is here if you want to take a look: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4915450/Grim\_Reach\_Idle/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4915450/Grim_Reach_Idle/)



Happy to answer questions about Steam or how I work.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
Hey, thank you! I worked around 2 months on Grim Reach, around 10 Hours a day probably. I was jobless at the time and wanted to make use of my free time. And i didn't market it at all, honestly, i did everything wrong. I launched the steam page, waited 2 weeks and instantly released the game into early access 1 day before the initial launch was planned.   

At first i thought this game wouldn't be looked at anyways, i just wanted to put it out, so i can say i have released something as this was a dream of mine. But it turned out that people really liked the game and what i've build. Everything was praised, the balance, the loops, the idle-ability as dumb as that sounds. And over the first few weeks i put out updates every 1-2 days. Implemented recommended features, fixed bugs and eventually it felt really ready! And even the looks were praised, even though it does look pretty AI. I generated all \~1500 images needed at the time with ChatGPT inside the browser, before i upgraded to a better workflow with Codex. Thats why some images still have a really bad quality that i will fix in the future. In my experience, most players don't really care if the game is AI as long as it is fun. 

What did help me tremendously is language support, my game is available in 7 languages all over the world and that drastically increased my sale numbers as most sales come from Asia and Europe.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
Honestly, i let claude handle it all. I planned translations from the beginning and told him to implement everything with Translation Strings in mind. And so he did, there were some scaling issues or overflowing. But Claude learned real fast how to test this and from that moment on, there were no issues. There was not a single report because of broken translations as of now. So trusting Claude 100% seemed to work. 

And yeah, i try. I care about this hobby and try my best. I'm already working on Game 2 and its way better quality wise. I learned alot f rom Grim Reach and im now able to use that for my second game, which feels refreshing.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
90% Was Agent Feedback, it was not easy to decide what would be "Fun" but we have placed a Goal for each archetype, everything that supported this goal was considered fun and progressive, while things slowing you down or forcing you to do things that are against your archetype made things less fun. 

A good example of a solution i implemented was the Hunting Skill. I had a player who wasn't that interested in Fighting but needed the ingredients to craft stuff he wanted to do. So i implemented a Hunting skill, requiring you to kill the enemy atleast once in a zone. Then you need bait you get from fishing at different tier levels and only with bait you can hunt in the zones, only enemies, you once killed before. So you can afk Enemy kills now, while incorperating other skills like here, fishing. 

The other 10% was a singular Playtester who liked Idle games and gave me honest feedback. But as with all free playtesters, the interest is not always 100% there.

How many wishlists did you have before launch? And do you know where most of your first customers came from? Steam’s own recommendations, Reddit, content creators, or somewhere else?

replies.author: Shalke97

My wishlists on EA launch were around 350 as you can see on the Chart. There are two spikes, one is my EA Launch (Because i was feeling the game was unfinished) and after an intense month of daily  implementing and fixing i took the game out of EA.) I think that is also part of the success, i had two bumps instead of only one. But i was hit with a negative review because of the short EA window. 

As for negative experience, not once. I didn't post in any non-ai Reddits. I disclosed the usage and people didn't care at all, there were even a few who thought the style was good and they like it alot. So key here is having a consistent style.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body:
Gamedev here. At least ten years ago. I remember people in the same Flash showcases as me having idle games and I called the idea stupid. What's the point of a game that you can't play?

Cookie clicker, Idle Heroes and Venture Capitalist were all idle games. You click manually until it goes automatically. And then you pay to speed it up. There's no end.

Turns out people have no time to play games. So they let the game run in the background and come back to counters going up. That's really it. Numbers go up, dopamine hits.

It's also relatively easy to make for developers because well, it's mostly just numbers going up.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
Hey, my workflow in the beginning was very flawed. Basically, i determined a style, worked on it with ChatGPT. I wanted a slightly stylzed but realistic approach to achieve a dark fantasy "diablo like" atmosphere. When i achieved that, i told him to cook up 10 reference images in that style so that i can attach those as style references. And thats where it started, i kept the style consistent by a lways attaching references. 

I switched to an automated Codox approach later on. My Claude Agent wrote up all the asset needed for the current thing i was working on. For example 26 Enemy sprites. I implemented a prompt system where he basically filled out everything so Codex knew what to generate. My Codex agent knew where all my Asset were lying around, so if it read the text file for 26 Enemy sprites, it would look into my folder with all the enemies, take them as referenz for style and began generating the 26 Sprites. Before delivering them to me, he needed to verify the cleanliness of the generated image. Like Alpha Channels with transparent backgrounds. If everything was checked, i got a message that it was done -> I manually checked everything and thats it. Thats how i do it to this day.

comments.author: Nervous-Car-9014
comments.body: Lucky, I put my first game on steam the other day. I used Claude for code review and error testing with some art being made by gpt. I am a solo dev with no budget but I wanted to see my idea made real. I did the "ai used declaration" as I wanted to be upfront. I got 3 positive reviews and one negative that was "I didn't notice AI was used, too bad could have been a good game" with 4 hours of play time.. and now that's the only one that gets "was this review helpful" checks... I put months into the game and now I'm stigmatized... I didn't copy anyones game or idea and put a lot of love into it and all it took was one person with only negative reviews on their steam profile...

replies.author: CPTNJCKSPRRW
replies.body:
Yeah the misplaced hatred people have for AI assisted development is just going to feed companies like Sony, EA, 2k, and Ubisoft. 
They are the only ones who can TRUELY afford to do everything manually with their workforce and money. 

They just use AI to cut corners and now everyone immediately hates you (AN INDEPENDENT DEV)for not wanting to write out 382 smoke tests by hand. 

Makes me wanna say:
"Ok bro, you come here and do it for free then I don't have the time, or skills"
(I use placeholder AI art since I KNOW I'm bad at it, maybe I'll find someone willing to replace them all by hand for cheap maybe not)

We see all the Fable 5.2 posts about "EA is cooked" because indie devs can now make AAA games without taking billions from players. 

Naw, REAL Gamers are cooked because HATERS just love having something to hate at all times 😂. 

Go back to hating EA, you don't need to buy the game but if it's CLEARLY labelled as agentically assisted don't review bomb it "out of the principal".

Who do you think you're ACTUALLY harming?
At this rate you're just making the rich get richer.

Well there's my rant, guess I'll go crowdfund a game so I can hire a studio to make it for me 😂💀
